t: Every antibiotic ever made has started failing. Not one has been an exception.

Resistance has appeared to every antibacterial drug ever deployed, usually within a few years of introduction. There are no exceptions, and the reason there are none is that the mechanism does not depend on anything about the drug.
sub: That is not bad luck. It is the same three conditions again.
You have run this machine four times already, on beetles, moths, immune cells and behaviour.

question: Could a drug be designed that resistance never develops to?
Is a resistance-proof antimicrobial achievable in principle?
options: Not while it kills some and spares others, and survivors breed
Yes, if the dose is high enough
stages.outcome: Not while it kills some and spares others, and survivors breed
note: Commit. Ask which of the three conditions a better molecule could remove.

t: The same machine as the beetles, with a drug doing the selecting. Try to break it.
Identical mechanism, different agent. Establish it, then remove one condition — and note that none of the three is a property of the drug.
goal: You can only stop it by taking away variation, heredity, or the difference in survival. A drug cannot do any of those.

The three conditions are properties of the bacterial population, not of the drug. No chemistry removes any of them, which is why the question of a resistance-proof antibiotic is not an engineering problem.

t: Resistance is natural selection with the medicine doing the choosing.
Antimicrobial resistance is selection: bacteria vary, the variation is heritable, and the drug makes survival depend on it. The outcome follows automatically.
The drug supplies only the third condition. Variation and heredity belong to the bacteria, so no property of the molecule can prevent resistance — only slow it.

Fleming said so in his 1945 Nobel lecture, before resistance was a clinical problem, because the mechanism made it inevitable. That is a prediction from theory, made in advance, and it was right — which is a better argument for taking the theory seriously than any retrospective explanation.
sub: So the aim is never to prevent it. It is to slow it down.
Every measure — finishing courses, narrow spectrum, combinations, reducing agricultural use — buys time and none of them stops it.
Combinations work by requiring two rare events at once, which multiplies two small probabilities.

That is why tuberculosis and HIV are treated with three or four drugs simultaneously. Resistance to one is likely; resistance to four arising in the same organism is not, and the arithmetic of multiplying small probabilities is the whole of the strategy.

q: Why can no drug be resistance-proof?
Why is resistance inevitable rather than a failure of drug design?
Which of the three conditions could chemistry remove?
options: The drug only supplies one of the three conditions; the bacteria supply the others
Because drugs are never strong enough
why: Bacteria already vary, and they already pass what they have to their offspring. All the drug adds is a reason for some to survive and others not. You cannot design away the first two.

Variation and heredity are properties of the bacterial population and exist before any drug arrives. The drug supplies only differential survival. No molecule can remove conditions it does not control.

None. That is the point of the question — chemistry acts only on the third condition, and removing it means the drug does not kill anything. The strongest version of the argument is that a drug which selects nothing is a drug that does nothing.

t: Resistant infections already kill more people a year than malaria.

Estimates put deaths directly attributable to antimicrobial resistance well over a million a year, with several million more where it contributed. Meanwhile few genuinely new classes have reached the clinic in decades, partly because a drug that should be used sparingly is a poor commercial proposition. The scientific problem and the economic one are different problems, and only one of them is being worked on hard.
